extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and parties in TTAB/trademark proceedings (practitioners litigating before the Board)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and evidentiary rules governing discovery (including ESI), timing, extensions, depositions, disclosures, and methods for making produced documents of record in proceedings before the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: ESI accessibility — party resisting discovery must show undue burden or cost
rubrics_metrics.description: When an adverse party seeks to compel production of ESI, the party resisting discovery must show that the material sought is "not reasonably accessible because of undue burden or cost."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If that showing is made, the burden shifts to the requesting party to show good cause for production. (See Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(B).) Examples and case law illustrating when materials were found not reasonably accessible are provided (e.g., Frito-Lay v. Princeton Vanguard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden-shift and good-cause analysis for not-reasonably-accessible ESI
rubrics_metrics.description: If resisting party proves ESI not reasonably accessible, the requesting party must demonstrate good cause for production of such ESI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In deciding if good cause exists, the Board considers whether (i) discovery sought is unreasonably cumulative/duplicative or obtainable from a more convenient/less burdensome/less expensive source; (ii) the requesting party had ample opportunity to obtain the information by discovery in the action; and (iii) the burden or expense of proposed discovery outweighs its likely benefit considering the needs of the case, amount in controversy, parties' resources, importance of issues, and importance of the discovery in resolving issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionality and limiting ESI discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequacy of ESI production is judged with increasing focus on proportionality and whether extensive ESI discovery is necessary and justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the Board's limited jurisdiction and narrow issues, burden and expense of e-discovery will weigh heavily against requiring production in most cases. Parties should be precise in requests and consider ways to significantly limit production expense (e.g., narrow requests, date ranges, custodians). (See Frito-Lay v. Princeton Vanguard.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sample vs full production
rubrics_metrics.description: Where full production would be unduly burdensome, production of representative samples may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board will require representative samples in many circumstances (e.g., many documents/ESI), but if full production is not burdensome (e.g., only a small number of documents), full production may be required. Case examples: Sunkist (representative invoices), Bison (full production not burdensome), Frito-Lay (representative samples of ESI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard protective order and substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings pending or commenced on or after August 31, 2007, the Board's standard protective order automatically applies absent an agreed substitute approved by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may agree to and submit a substitute protective order for Board approval. The standard order provisions (e.g., limiting disclosure of confidential information) apply unless changed by Board-approved agreement. (37 CFR § 2.116(g))

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of customer names and confidentiality rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally the Board's policy is not to require disclosure of customer and mailing lists; parties need not reveal customer names unless the issue (e.g., abandonment or first use) makes such disclosure necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where disclosure is necessary, protective orders can limit disclosure (e.g., to attorneys only). Cases cited: Johnston Pump (identify classes of customers sufficient unless issue requires names), Fisons (need for names may outweigh confidentiality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege and work-product assertions — required form
rubrics_metrics.description: A party making a claim of privilege must do so expressly and describe the nature of the withheld information as provided in Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attorney-client privilege provides absolute protection unless waived; work-product protection is qualified and may be overcome by a showing of need/undue hardship, with a higher burden for mental impressions. Disclosure to third parties can waive privilege. Case examples: In re Seagate; Genentech v. ITC; Red Wing v. Smucker.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery period — Board-set schedule and length
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will specify deadlines for a discovery conference, opening and closing dates for discovery, and deadlines within the discovery period for initial and expert disclosures; the discovery period is set for 180 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The trial order setting deadlines is included with the notice of institution. Parties may stipulate to shorten or extend the discovery period (subject to Board approval or motion). The opening of discovery coincides with the discovery conference deadline for cases on/after Nov. 1, 2007.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and taking of discovery must occur on or before discovery close
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be taken, and interrogatories, requests for production, and requests for admission must be served on or before the closing date of the discovery period as originally set or as reset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests may be served until the close date, but depositions must also be taken during the period (unless parties stipulate otherwise or Board orders otherwise). Combined notices that require deponents to bring documents must account for response time (normally at least 35 days before close).

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial disclosures prerequisite for discovery (post-November 1, 2007 cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: For cases commenced on or after November 1, 2007, a serving party must have made its initial disclosures prior to seeking discovery absent a stipulation or Board order to the contrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written discovery may be served concurrently with initial disclosures. A party cannot notice depositions until it has served initial disclosures unless disclosures are waived. Failure to make initial disclosures can result in denial of motions to compel. (See Dating DNA v. Imagini; 37 CFR § 2.120(a)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time to respond to discovery requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Responses to interrogatories, requests for production, and requests for admission must be served within thirty days from the date of service of such discovery requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If service is by first-class mail/Express Mail/overnight courier, the date of mailing/delivery is the service date and five extra days are allowed for responding; if parties agree to electronic service, the five-day grace period does not apply. See Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(b)(2), 34(b)(2)(A), 36(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: No discovery-priority rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery in Board proceedings is not governed by any concept of priority of right to take discovery or depositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being first to serve requests does not entitle a party to receive responses before it must respond to adversary's subsequently served requests; each party must respond within time allowed irrespective of sequence. Parties are encouraged to initiate discovery early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections — merits vs. characteristics-based objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections to discovery that go to the merits include relevance, overbreadth, vagueness, ambiguity, burdensomeness, or not reasonably calculated to lead to admissible evidence; objections based on privilege/confidentiality/work product concern characteristics of the information sought rather than the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merits objections can be forfeited by failure to timely respond. Privilege claims must be asserted expressly and described per Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failing to respond timely
rubrics_metrics.description: A party failing to respond to interrogatories or document requests during the allowed time, and unable to show excusable neglect, may be found to have forfeited its right to object to the discovery request on its merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For requests for admissions, a party may move to reopen time due to excusable neglect (Fed. R. Civ. P. 6(b)(1)(B)) or move to withdraw/amend admissions under Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(b). Case examples: No Fear Inc. v. Rule; Envirotech v. Compagnie Des Lampes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions — how obtained and effect on other deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery period or time to respond may be extended upon stipulation of the parties approved by the Board, by motion granted by the Board, or by order of the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resetting the closing date for discovery will result in rescheduling of pretrial disclosure deadlines and testimony periods automatically. However, extending time to respond to a discovery request does not automatically reschedule other deadlines (expert disclosures, close of discovery, testimony periods) unless the parties stipulate and the Board approves or the Board orders it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stipulations to extend or reopen — filing form and Board approval
rubrics_metrics.description: When parties stipulate to reschedule pretrial disclosures/testimony periods or to reschedule the closing date for discovery, the stipulation should be presented in the form used in a trial order, signed by the parties, or as a motion in that form signed by one party and stating other parties' agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stipulation to extend only response time may not always need to be filed, but if it interferes with orderly completion of discovery or opening of trial, Board approval is required. It is recommended stipulations be reduced to writing even if not filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-cause standard for extensions — when delay may or may not justify extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere delay in initiating discovery does not constitute good cause for extension; parties waiting until the end of the discovery window will not be heard to complain if follow-up discovery is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversely, if a responding party delays or responds improperly forcing the propounding party to move to compel, that delay or improper response can constitute good cause, and the Board will extend discovery at least for the propounding party to restore the time that would have remained had responses been timely and proper. Case examples: Miss America Pageant; Neville Chemical Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods to make produced documents of record
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents produced in response to requests or through disclosures may not be made of record by notice of reliance alone except to the extent they qualify as printed publications or official records under 37 CFR § 2.122(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three methods to make produced documents of record if they do not qualify under § 2.122(e): (1) Serve a request for admission of genuineness (with exhibits) before discovery closes and later file notice of reliance on the admission during the testimony period; (2) Take a discovery deposition marking documents as exhibits and have a witness identify them, then submit the deposition and exhibits during testimony under notice of reliance; (3) Serve a combined request for production and notice of deposition asking the deponent to bring documents to the deposition (must account for thirty-day response plus five-day mail grace — normally serve at least 35 days before close). Parties may also stipulate that any party may introduce another party's produced documents by notice of reliance, subject to objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publications and official records via notice of reliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Printed publications and official records that are competent evidence and relevant may be introduced in evidence by filing a notice of reliance specifying the publication/record, source and date, pages to be read, general relevance, and accompanied by the copy or official record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A copy of an official PTO record need not be certified. The notice of reliance shall be filed during the testimony period of the party filing the notice. (37 CFR § 2.122(e))

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery depositions — timing, notice, and who may take them
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery depositions must be both noticed and taken prior to expiration of the discovery period (unless parties stipulate otherwise). Discovery depositions generally may be taken by any party of any adverse party or any relevant non-party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a matter of convenience and courtesy, parties should attempt to schedule depositions by agreement rather than unilaterally setting dates. Depositions must be taken during the discovery period; notice alone is insufficient if the deposition occurs after the close. Case examples: National Football League v. DNH Management; Smith International v. Olin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may be deposed under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(a), a party may, by oral questions, depose any person, including a party, without leave of court except as provided in Rule 30(a)(2); attendance may be compelled by subpoena under Rule 45.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leave of court is required where Rule 30(a)(2) applies; leave must be granted to the extent consistent with limits in Rule 26(b)(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate in scheduling and conducting discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have a duty to cooperate in resolving conflicts in scheduling and taking depositions and in discovery generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board expects parties to work out mutually agreeable schedules for depositions and to cooperate in discovery to avoid unnecessary motions or delays. Case examples: Sunrider v. Raats; Luehrmann v. Kwik Kopy.
